meaning: The sacred utterance that became the Absolute — the power of prayer expanded into the world-ground of the Upaniṣads

phonemes.desc: The ā is long “ah”; the h following the m is aspirated breath — brah-, not bram-.
Short final vowel; the neuter noun names the absolute itself.
Final n is lightly sounded; in the nominative the stem is brahma.

kin.label: Vedic
kin.form: brahman — the sacred utterance, the formula

kin.label: Later sense
kin.form: the Absolute, the world-ground of the Upaniṣads

pronunciation.note: The word rises through three meanings: the spoken verse, the ritual power, and finally the all — the history of Indian metaphysics in one noun.

domains.title: The Absolute, the World-Ground
domains.subtitle: The Sacred Utterance That Became the All
domains.lead: Brahman is the load-bearing concept of Indian thought: the absolute reality beneath gods, world, and self. The word begins as the Vedic priest’s formula — the verse whose correct utterance moves the cosmos — and ends as the Upaniṣads’ world-ground, that which speech cannot reach but without which no speech sounds. In the lexicon it stands for the principle personified: not a god among gods, but what the gods are made of.

cards.name: The Utterance
cards.desc: The Vedic brahman is the spoken formula — the verse whose pronunciation is ritual power.

cards.name: The World-Ground
cards.desc: In the Upaniṣads, brahman is the all: “from which words turn back, together with the mind, unable to reach it”.

cards.name: Tat Tvam Asi
cards.desc: “That thou art”: the Chandogya’s equation of brahman and the self — the tradition’s most quoted sentence.

cards.name: Not This, Not This
cards.desc: Neti neti — the negative path: brahman defined by what it is not, since it is everything that is.

mythology.lead: Brahman has no myths — it is what myths are made of. Its ‘stories’ are the doctrine’s own ascent: the Vedic priest’s formula becoming the cosmic principle, the forest sages’ equation of the self with the all, and the grammarians’ discovery that the sacred syllable AUM is brahman compressed into sound.

myths.title: The Creation Hymn
myths.text: The Nāsadīya sūkta contemplates the state before creation — ‘there was neither existence nor non-existence’ — and names the One that breathed without breath. The hymn refuses to say what that One is; the later tradition named it brahman, and built the Upaniṣadic quest on the hymn’s silence.

myths.title: Brahman as Food
myths.text: The Taittirīya builds the cosmos from nourishment: food is brahman, the eater is brahman, the eater of the eater is brahman. The sequence — food, breath, mind, knowledge, bliss — is the Upaniṣadic ladder of the self, each rung a thicker description of the absolute.

myths.title: Tat Tvam Asi
myths.text: Nine times the teacher Uddālaka tells his son Śvetaketu ‘tat tvam asi’ — that thou art — reasoning from salt dissolved in water: invisible, present everywhere, the ground of taste. The sentence became the keystone of Vedānta, quoted by every commentator from Śaṅkara to the modern sages.

myths.title: Neti Neti
myths.text: The great dialogue has Yājñavalkya answer the question ‘what is brahman?’ only by negations — neti neti, not this, not this. The method is the tradition’s most honest: the absolute cannot be described, only approached by stripping away every description. The gods, the world, and the self remain — as its body.

lore.syncretism: Brahman absorbed every rival absolute: the Vedic ṛta, the Upaniṣadic ātman, the grammarian’s śabda, and — through the Vedānta commentaries — the personal gods themselves, who turned out to be brahman’s named aspects. Buddhism defined its nirvāṇa partly against brahman, which kept the concept honest; and modern Indian philosophy still uses the word for the ultimate in any school.
lore.culturalLegacy: The word gave India its most quoted sentence (‘tat tvam asi’), its most quoted method (‘neti neti’), and its most quoted sound (AUM). ‘Brahman’ passed into English as the learned word for the absolute; and the identification of brahman and ātman remains, after a century of translation, the central puzzle of comparative philosophy — the self and the world, one or two.
lore.extendedMeditation: Brahman: the name that refuses to be a name. Restored plainly, it demonstrates the lexicon’s wager — that plain letters can carry what the Upaniṣads said words cannot carry. Say it, and the utterance is the thing: a two-syllable formula older than the temples built to out-shout it.
lore.archaeology: Brahman leaves no temple — it is the reason temples are redundant. Its monuments are manuscripts: the Upaniṣads’ palm-leaf lines, the Vedānta commentaries’ endless recursion, and the syllable AUM carved over every doorway of the tradition.
lore.cult: Its liturgy is recitation: the Veda read aloud is brahman’s daily performance. The upanayana initiation — the thread-ceremony — admits a boy to the utterance; every subsequent recitation keeps the absolute in circulation.
lore.iconography: AUM is brahman’s only image — the three curves and the dot, mapped by the tradition onto waking, dream, deep sleep, and the absolute. Where a temple must show something, it shows the syllable.
lore.reception: Arthur Schopenhauer called the Upaniṣadic brahman the highest product of human thought before Kant; theosophy and then physics popularized it (‘the universe is brahman’ reads like an early draft of certain cosmologies). The word entered the world’s philosophical vocabulary — the absolute that needs no capital letter.
